# Requirements and architecture: the loop problem

Research notes for my workflow: the known problem behind "it's a loop, not a straight line", and the established ways to handle it. Companion to my note on my spec-driven development agentic workflow.

> [!summary] TL;DR
> - **The problem is old and well known.** What a system must do and how it's built shape each other, so neither can be finished first. Swartout & Balzer named it for software in 1982: the "inevitable intertwining of specification and implementation". Nuseibeh's "Twin Peaks" (2001) is the usual name for the requirements-and-architecture version.
> - **No established approach removes the loop. They manage it**, in three ways: iterate, but keep the documents separate; put a technology-free interface between the problem and the solution; and make every design decision explicit, with an owner.
> - **Closest fits for my workflow:** Zave & Jackson's requirements–specification model, which backs a technology-free contract and splits obligations between the person who needs the system and whoever builds it; Twin Peaks iteration with Parnas & Clements' rule that a decision only counts once it's in the right document; and decision records with a proposed/accepted status.
> - **Caveats:** "architecture-agnostic" is always relative to some set of alternatives; a technology-free contract can still be forced to change by what turns out to be buildable; and practitioners report the line between "what" and "how" is hard to hold.

## The problem

Terms used below:

- **Requirements:** what's needed.
- **Architecture:** the high-level structure and technology of the solution.
- **Specification:** a precise description of what to build. In my workflow, the contract is the closest match.
- **Interface:** where the system meets its users and the world.

### Where it was first stated

- **Swartout & Balzer (1982), software.** "Contrary to recent claims that specification should be completed before implementation begins, this paper presents two arguments that the two processes must be intertwined."
  - "Limitations of available implementation technology may force a specification change." Their example: a stack built on an array gets a maximum depth.
  - "Implementation choices may suggest augmentations to the original specification." Their example: reusing a pattern-matching routine adds wildcards to an editor's search.
- **Rittel & Webber (1973), planning.** "Wicked problems" have no definitive formulation: "The information needed to understand the problem depends upon one's idea for solving it." "Problem understanding and problem resolution are concomitant to each other." They wrote about social policy, but design fields widely borrow the idea.
- **Parnas & Clements (1986).** No project follows the ideal top-down order. One of their reasons: "Many of the details only become known to us as we progress in the implementation. Some of the things that we learn invalidate our design and we must backtrack."
- **Brooks (1987).** "It is really impossible for clients, even those working with software engineers, to specify completely, precisely, and correctly the exact requirements of a modern software product before having built and tried some versions of the product they are specifying."

### How it's framed today

- **Twin Peaks (Nuseibeh 2001).** Requirements and architecture are two peaks, developed "concurrently" and interleaved, each getting more detailed over time.
  - Starting from only one of them gives "artificially frozen requirements documents", or architectures that resist "inevitable and desirable changes in requirements".
  - "Candidate architectures may constrain what requirements can be met, and of course the choice of requirements impacts the architecture selected or developed."
  - Yet their "distinct content is preserved": problem and solution stay separate.
- **Problem–solution co-evolution (design research).** Maher, Poon & Boulanger (1996) modelled design as problem and solution spaces evolving together. Dorst & Cross (2001) studied nine experienced industrial designers and "confirm[ed] the general validity" of that model.
- **Architecturally significant requirements (ASRs).** The requirements that most shape the architecture, often quality needs such as security, performance and reliability. A 2013 IEEE Software special issue on Twin Peaks says these "drive and constrain a system's architectural design". Chen, Ali Babar & Nuseibeh (2013) characterized ASRs from interviews with 90 practitioners.

> [!note] Link to my earlier thought
> "The contract changes depending on mobile versus web" is a Swartout & Balzer case: an implementation choice reshaping the specification.

## Known approaches

### At a glance

| Approach | Key idea | What it does about the loop |
|---|---|---|
| Twin Peaks | Develop requirements and architecture together | Iterates, but keeps them as separate documents |
| "Fake it" (Parnas & Clements) | Iterate in practice, document as if top-down | Every change lands in the right document |
| Axiomatic design (Suh) | Alternate requirement and design at each level | Makes the loop explicit, one level at a time |
| Set-based design (Toyota) | Keep several designs open, narrow slowly | Delays commitment until there's evidence |
| Zave & Jackson's model | The spec covers only behaviour at the interface | A fixed, technology-free middle layer |
| Problem frames (Jackson) | Describe the problem in the world, not the machine | Same idea, later extended to admit architecture |
| Information hiding, ADTs, Design by Contract | Interfaces hide decisions likely to change | Technology choices stay behind the interface |
| Ports and adapters, Clean Architecture | The core talks through technology-free ports | UI and storage become swappable adapters |
| Model-Driven Architecture (OMG) | Platform-independent model first | Separates "what" from "on which platform" |
| Specification by Example | Examples describe behaviour, not clicks | Specs survive implementation changes |
| SEI methods (scenarios, ADD, ATAM) | Measurable quality scenarios drive design | Makes design drivers and constraints explicit |
| Architecture decision records | One short record per significant decision | Each decision is visible, with a status |
| Arcadia (systems engineering) | Need analysis, then logical, then physical design | The customer approves the need; engineers own the design |
| Spec Kit, Kiro (AI tools) | Separate the spec from the technical plan | Gates, clarification markers, re-sync after changes |

### Twin Peaks

- **What:** requirements and architecture as two peaks, worked on at the same time. Nuseibeh describes it as a finer-grained version of Boehm's spiral model (1988).
- **Loop:** accepts it. Early solution work surfaces requirements, which suits what Boehm (2000) called IKIWISI ("I'll know it when I see it").
- **Useful idea:** "core requirements", the goals likely to last longest, which should anchor a stable architecture.
- **Trade-offs:** a stance more than a method. It says to iterate and keep the content separate, not how to decide or who decides.

### "A rational design process: how and why to fake it" (Parnas & Clements 1986)

- **What:** nobody designs top-down, but you produce and maintain the documents that an ideal top-down process would have produced.
- **Loop:** iterate freely. When something you learn invalidates a document, fix it and every document after it. "The documentation is our medium of design and no design decisions are considered to be made until their incorporation into the documents."
- **Rules useful here:**
  - Every requirements statement "should be valid for all acceptable products; none should depend on implementation decisions."
  - Gaps "should be explicitly indicated".
  - Developers "produce a draft document and get it reviewed and, eventually, approved by the user representatives."
- **Trade-offs:** the documents need constant upkeep, and they deliberately hide the messy history, so rationale needs its own home.

### Axiomatic design (Suh)

- **What:** requirements (functional requirements, FRs) and design (design parameters, DPs) are broken down together. A requirement can only be broken down after choosing the design that meets it: "Having chosen the DP1, we can now decompose FR1."
- **Loop:** a disciplined zigzag: requirement, then design, then sub-requirements, then sub-designs.
- **Trade-offs:** from mechanical engineering, and formal (design matrices). It implies that deep requirement trees inevitably carry design decisions.

### Set-based concurrent engineering (Toyota)

- **What:** keep sets of design options open and narrow them gradually. Toyota "considers a broader range of possible designs and delays certain decisions longer than other automotive companies do, yet has what may be the fastest and most efficient vehicle development cycles in the industry."
- **Loop:** avoids picking one design early and then patching it, which fails if "one picks the wrong starting point".
- **Principles** (wording from secondary sources): map the design space; integrate by intersection; establish feasibility before commitment.
- **Trade-offs:** exploring several options costs more up front. Built for car development with many teams.

### Requirements, domain knowledge and specification (Zave & Jackson; Gunter et al.)

- **What:** three kinds of description.
  - **Requirements:** what we want to become true in the world.
  - **Domain knowledge:** what's true of the world regardless of the system, i.e. assumptions.
  - **Specification:** the system's behaviour at its interface with the world, using only what both sides can observe ("shared phenomena").
  - **The test:** specification + domain knowledge ⊢ requirements. (⊢ means "together guarantee".)
- **Loop:** the specification is a stable middle layer. "To say anything else about the machine is regarded as implementation bias." "It is not necessary or desirable to describe (however abstractly) the machine to be built."
- **Ownership:** Gunter et al. split the obligations. The buyer answers for the environment side: the domain knowledge holds, and specification plus domain knowledge give the requirements. The seller answers for the system side: the program meets the specification. "They build their deal around S, which serves as their basis of communication."
- **On restating:** "Some requirements are already implementable, so they can be copied directly from R to S." The others differ because they mention things the system can't observe or control, and domain knowledge bridges that gap.
- **Trade-offs:** formal roots (logic). And where the interface sits is itself a choice: Zave & Jackson say their framework characterizes the results of exploring that boundary, "not the explorations themselves", citing Swartout & Balzer.

### Problem frames (Jackson)

- **What:** analyse the problem in the world, not in the machine. "The intrinsic domain properties bridge the gap between the phenomena mentioned in the requirement and the phenomena directly accessible to the machine at its external interface to the world."
- **Loop:** keeps attention on the problem. Hall et al. (2002) found that "even modestly complex problems can force us into detailed consideration of the architecture of the solution", so they extended problem frames to allow "architectural structures, services and artifacts to be considered as part of the problem domain".
- **Trade-offs:** the notation and catalogue of frames take learning. The 2002 extension concedes that existing architecture sometimes belongs in the problem.

### Information hiding, abstract data types, Design by Contract

- **What:**
  - Parnas (1972): start from "a list of difficult design decisions or design decisions which are likely to change", and give each module an interface "chosen to reveal as little as possible about its inner workings".
  - Liskov & Zilles (1974): abstract data types, used only through their operations.
  - Meyer (1992): a contract states what the caller must provide and what the supplier guarantees (preconditions and postconditions). It "protects the client by specifying how much should be done" and the contractor "by specifying how little is acceptable".
- **Loop:** decisions likely to change sit behind an interface, so changing them leaves the interface alone.
- **Trade-offs:** module-level ideas. Scaling them to a whole product's interface, and choosing the right interface, are judgment calls.

### Ports and adapters (Cockburn), Clean Architecture (Martin)

- **What:** the application talks to the world through "ports", each "a purposeful conversation". Technology-specific "adapters" plug into them. "A graphical user interface or GUI is an example of an adapter." Martin: "A Web UI could be replaced with a console UI, for example, without changing the business rules."
- **Loop:** use cases "should generally be written at the application boundary... regardless of external technology", which makes them "more stable over time".
- **Trade-offs:** "What exactly a port is and isn't is largely a matter of taste." Qualities that live in an adapter, such as look and feel, fall outside a port-level description.

### Model-Driven Architecture (OMG)

- **What:** a computation-independent model (the domain and its requirements), a platform-independent model (PIM: the system without a platform), and platform-specific models (PSM).
- **Loop:** separates the platform choice from the system's logic. One PIM can target several technologies.
- **Trade-offs:** independence is relative. "What counts as a platform is relative to the purpose of the modeler"; "the concepts of PIM and PSM are, therefore, relative." Böckeler notes model-driven development "never took off for business applications, it sits at an awkward abstraction level and just creates too much overhead and constraints."

### Declarative scenarios, Specification by Example

- **What:** concrete examples, often written as Given/When/Then, describe behaviour rather than steps through a UI. Cucumber's test for each line: "Will this wording need to change if the implementation does?" If so, rewrite it. "What if, in the future, users log in with a voice interface or a thumbprint?"
- **Loop:** the examples stay valid through big implementation changes. Adzic reports teams relying on these "living documentation" suites to rebuild core systems; one team "had to rewrite the core of the virtual agent engine from scratch".
- **Trade-offs:** staying declarative takes discipline, and examples cover cases, not everything.

### SEI methods: quality attribute scenarios, ADD, ATAM

- **What:**
  - **Quality attribute scenario:** "a short description of how a system is required to respond to some stimulus", in six parts: source, stimulus, artifact, environment, response, response measure.
  - **Attribute-Driven Design (ADD):** design the architecture in iterations from "architectural drivers": design purpose, quality attributes, primary functionality, architectural concerns and constraints. "A constraint is a decision over which you have little or no control as an architect", such as "mandated technologies".
  - **ATAM** (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method): evaluates a candidate architecture against prioritized scenarios to find risks and trade-offs. (Summary from secondary sources.)
- **Loop:** quality needs are stated in a measurable, technology-free form, then drive the architecture and test it.
- **Trade-offs:** heavyweight for small projects; the workshops and evaluations assume teams of people.

### Architecture decision records (ADRs)

- **What:** one short file per "architecturally significant" decision: "those that affect the structure, non-functional characteristics, dependencies, interfaces, or construction techniques". Sections: title, context, decision, status, consequences.
- **Loop:** "Not all decisions will be made at once, nor will all of them be done when the project begins." Records are added as decisions are made, and a reversed decision is marked "superseded" rather than deleted.
- **Ownership:** the status records agreement: "proposed" until the stakeholders agree, then "accepted".
- **Trade-offs:** only works if writing them is routine, and it doesn't say who decides.

### Arcadia (systems engineering)

- **What:** a model-based method from Thales, now an AFNOR standard, with "a clear distinction between need and solution". Its levels: operational need analysis; system need analysis (what the system does at its boundary with users and other systems); logical architecture (a "notional solution"); and physical architecture, where "technical and technological constraints and choices" come in.
- **Loop:** one of its golden rules: "Check requirements against an architectural design model (early architecture) for robustness and feasibility." Need analysis can "renegotiate" customer requirements.
- **Ownership:** the two need-analysis levels "'specify' the subsequent design, and therefore should be approved/validated with the Customer."
- **Trade-offs:** built for large systems engineering with model tooling (Capella).

### AI spec-driven tools: Spec Kit and Kiro (docs read October 2026)

- **GitHub Spec Kit:**
  - The spec (what and why) is separate from the plan (how). The spec template says to "Avoid HOW to implement (no tech stack, APIs, code structure)", and that success criteria "must be technology-agnostic and measurable". The plan names the project type ("library/cli/web-service/mobile-app/…") and holds the technical "contracts/".
  - Anything unclear becomes "[NEEDS CLARIFICATION: specific question]" rather than a guess.
  - Feedback runs both ways: "When an architect discovers a better pattern, the PRD updates to reflect new possibilities." It also offers "Branching for Exploration: Generate multiple implementation approaches from the same specification".
- **Kiro:**
  - Three files with an approval gate after each: requirements.md (in EARS form: "WHEN … THE SYSTEM SHALL …"), design.md (architecture, interfaces, data models) and tasks.md.
  - Two workflows: Requirements-First and Design-First. Its docs suggest a Design-First spec "to validate technical feasibility", then a Requirements-First spec "for full feature development". After design changes, it can "validate and regenerate requirements to ensure they remain feasible".
- **Practitioner caution (Böckeler 2025):** separating the functional spec from the technical one is the common aim, but "I don't think we have a good track record as a profession to do this well."

## How this could map to my workflow

> [!warning] Interpretation, not findings
> Everything above is what the sources say. This section applies it to my workflow as options with trade-offs. It doesn't recommend one.

### Vocabulary match

| Zave & Jackson, Gunter et al. | My workflow |
|---|---|
| Requirements (wanted properties of the world) | Requirements tree |
| Domain knowledge (assumptions about the world) | No explicit home today |
| Specification (behaviour at the interface) | Contract |
| Program on a platform | Implementation, including architecture and tech stack |

### (a) An architecture-agnostic contract

**Support in the sources:**

- Zave & Jackson's specification: only shared phenomena, no "implementation bias".
- Parnas' information hiding: hide the decisions most likely to change, and the platform is one of them.
- Cockburn's ports: a GUI is an adapter, so mobile versus web sits outside the contract. My note's to-do example (add a task, list open tasks, mark a task done) has the shape of ports, or of an abstract data type's operations.
- Martin's "independent of UI", MDA's platform-independent model, Spec Kit's technology-agnostic success criteria, and the rewrites in Specification by Example.

**What the sources say about the risk of restating the requirements:**

- **Some overlap is fine.** Requirements already stated at the interface can be "copied directly from R to S" (Zave & Jackson). Parnas & Clements' requirements document is itself a black-box description of the system's outputs, with no separate contract for the whole system.
- **They differ when requirements are about the world.** If my requirements describe my needs in the world and the contract describes the interface, the two shouldn't collapse into one, provided the assumptions linking them are written down.
- **Limits:**
  - "Agnostic" is relative to some set of platforms (MDA).
  - A technology-free contract can still be forced to change by what turns out to be buildable (Swartout & Balzer).
  - Where to draw the interface is itself a choice (Zave & Jackson).
  - The line is hard to hold in practice (Böckeler).

**Options:**

1. **Write domain assumptions next to the requirements**, for example "I check my task list every morning". Requirements, assumptions and contract can then be checked against each other.
   - For: shows why the contract isn't a restatement, and makes the human's side checkable (Gunter et al.).
   - Against: one more thing to write and keep current.
2. **Say what the contract is agnostic to**, for example "the same on a phone, in a browser or in a terminal".
   - For: makes "agnostic" checkable, since independence is relative (MDA).
   - Against: can rule out an option nobody thought to list.
3. **Use Cucumber's question as the rule for contract lines:** would this line change if the architecture changed? If so, it doesn't belong in the contract.
   - For: cheap, and easy for agents to apply.
   - Against: judgment calls at the edges, such as look and feel.
4. **Write contract lines as declarative Given/When/Then scenarios.**
   - For: they double as acceptance tests and survive rewrites.
   - Against: longer than a list of operations.
5. **Write needs that shape the architecture as quality scenarios in the requirements** (stimulus, response, measure). For example: with no network, the human can still add a task within a second.
   - For: if mobile versus web matters because of a need, the need is stated and the agent still picks the architecture.
   - Against: takes care to keep solution words out of the scenario.

### (b) Keeping architecture decisions with their owner

**What the sources do:**

- Make the split explicit: the buyer owns "specification + domain knowledge give the requirements", the seller owns "the program meets the specification" (Gunter et al.).
- A decision only exists once it's written in its document (Parnas & Clements).
- Mark unknowns instead of guessing (Parnas & Clements' explicit gaps; Spec Kit's NEEDS CLARIFICATION markers).
- A technology choice someone else imposes enters only as a named constraint, separate from the requirements (ADD). My workflow already does this: steering is the only place I name a technology.
- Record significant decisions with a status, proposed then accepted (Nygard).
- The customer approves the need analysis; engineers own the logical and physical architecture (Arcadia).
- **Warning from axiomatic design:** below the top levels, breaking a requirement down takes a design choice. A deep requirements tree can quietly carry design decisions, the same leak I worried about in the contract.

**Options:**

1. **Adopt the Gunter et al. split as my ownership rule.** Human: requirements, assumptions and contract together give what I need. Agent: the implementation meets the contract.
   - For: precise, and matches my ownership table.
   - Against: the human side is only checkable with written assumptions, as in (a) option 1.
2. **Decision records with a status.** The agent proposes architecture decisions as records, and steering says which ones need my acceptance.
   - For: every architecture decision is visible, with an audit trail. It's also a possible home for the agent's reason when it departs from a FAVOR or DISFAVOR.
   - Against: overhead, and the risk of rubber-stamping.
3. **Mark, don't assume.** While helping draft the requirements or the contract, an agent flags any line that would assume an architecture instead of writing it.
   - For: cheap, and catches leaks where they start.
   - Against: depends on the agent noticing.
4. **Stop breaking down a requirement when the next level would need a design choice.** It stays "sufficient as stated", and the detail becomes the agent's.
   - For: keeps the tree free of design decisions, and fits my rule of breaking down only when needed.
   - Against: requirements may stay vaguer than I'd like.

### (c) Where the loop could live in the agentic software factory

**What the sources do:** iterate with separate documents (Twin Peaks); build and try versions to learn (Brooks); check requirements against an early architecture (Arcadia, Kiro's Design-First); keep several options open (set-based design, Spec Kit's branching); and update every affected document after a change (Parnas & Clements, Kiro's re-sync).

**Options.** None of these names a tech stack:

1. **Feasibility probe before the contract is agreed.** The agent tries throwaway sketches of candidate architectures against the draft requirements and contract, then reports what's infeasible and what it would suggest. I decide.
   - For: catches unbuildable contracts early, Swartout & Balzer's first case.
   - Against: costs agent time, and a sketch can anchor the choice.
2. **Change requests upward during implementation.** When the agent hits a limit that forces a change, or makes a choice that suggests an addition, it stops and proposes a change to the right artifact (requirement, assumption, contract or steering) instead of adapting quietly. This extends my existing "stop and ask the human" rule.
   - For: the loop runs through me, so ownership holds.
   - Against: more interruptions.
3. **Keep the documents current.** After any accepted change, the agent updates every affected document so the specification reads as if it had been derived top-down (Parnas & Clements).
   - For: the specification stays trustworthy. That matters more in my workflow because I never edit the implementation, which Böckeler calls "spec-as-source"; she warns it may combine the inflexibility of model-driven development with the non-determinism of LLMs.
   - Against: ongoing maintenance.
4. **Keep options open.** The agent carries two or three architecture candidates until evidence picks one.
   - For: avoids early lock-in (set-based design).
   - Against: more work per feature.

All four need somewhere in the project environment to record proposed changes and decisions with a status. That could become part of the contract between the factory and the environment, alongside "some ticketing system".

## Sources

How each was checked: **read** (full text, or the relevant part), **abstract** (abstract only), **citation** (details confirmed, content not read).

### The problem

# Requirements and architecture: the loop problem

Research notes for my workflow: the known problem behind "it's a loop, not a straight line", and the established ways to handle it. Companion to my note on my spec-driven development agentic workflow.

> [!summary] TL;DR
> - **The problem is old and well known.** What a system must do and how it's built shape each other, so neither can be finished first. Swartout & Balzer named it for software in 1982: the "inevitable intertwining of specification and implementation". Nuseibeh's "Twin Peaks" (2001) is the usual name for the requirements-and-architecture version.
> - **No established approach removes the loop. They manage it**, in three ways: iterate, but keep the documents separate; put a technology-free interface between the problem and the solution; and make every design decision explicit, with an owner.
> - **Closest fits for my workflow:** Zave & Jackson's requirements–specification model, which backs a technology-free contract and splits obligations between the person who needs the system and whoever builds it; Twin Peaks iteration with Parnas & Clements' rule that a decision only counts once it's in the right document; and decision records with a proposed/accepted status.
> - **Caveats:** "architecture-agnostic" is always relative to some set of alternatives; a technology-free contract can still be forced to change by what turns out to be buildable; and practitioners report the line between "what" and "how" is hard to hold.

## The problem

Terms used below:

- **Requirements:** what's needed.
- **Architecture:** the high-level structure and technology of the solution.
- **Specification:** a precise description of what to build. In my workflow, the contract is the closest match.
- **Interface:** where the system meets its users and the world.

### Where it was first stated

- **Swartout & Balzer (1982), software.** "Contrary to recent claims that specification should be completed before implementation begins, this paper presents two arguments that the two processes must be intertwined."
  - "Limitations of available implementation technology may force a specification change." Their example: a stack built on an array gets a maximum depth.
  - "Implementation choices may suggest augmentations to the original specification." Their example: reusing a pattern-matching routine adds wildcards to an editor's search.
- **Rittel & Webber (1973), planning.** "Wicked problems" have no definitive formulation: "The information needed to understand the problem depends upon one's idea for solving it." "Problem understanding and problem resolution are concomitant to each other." They wrote about social policy, but design fields widely borrow the idea.
- **Parnas & Clements (1986).** No project follows the ideal top-down order. One of their reasons: "Many of the details only become known to us as we progress in the implementation. Some of the things that we learn invalidate our design and we must backtrack."
- **Brooks (1987).** "It is really impossible for clients, even those working with software engineers, to specify completely, precisely, and correctly the exact requirements of a modern software product before having built and tried some versions of the product they are specifying."

### How it's framed today

- **Twin Peaks (Nuseibeh 2001).** Requirements and architecture are two peaks, developed "concurrently" and interleaved, each getting more detailed over time.
  - Starting from only one of them gives "artificially frozen requirements documents", or architectures that resist "inevitable and desirable changes in requirements".
  - "Candidate architectures may constrain what requirements can be met, and of course the choice of requirements impacts the architecture selected or developed."
  - Yet their "distinct content is preserved": problem and solution stay separate.
- **Problem–solution co-evolution (design research).** Maher, Poon & Boulanger (1996) modelled design as problem and solution spaces evolving together. Dorst & Cross (2001) studied nine experienced industrial designers and "confirm[ed] the general validity" of that model.
- **Architecturally significant requirements (ASRs).** The requirements that most shape the architecture, often quality needs such as security, performance and reliability. A 2013 IEEE Software special issue on Twin Peaks says these "drive and constrain a system's architectural design". Chen, Ali Babar & Nuseibeh (2013) characterized ASRs from interviews with 90 practitioners.

> [!note] Link to my earlier thought
> "The contract changes depending on mobile versus web" is a Swartout & Balzer case: an implementation choice reshaping the specification.

## Known approaches

### At a glance

| Approach | Key idea | What it does about the loop |
|---|---|---|
| Twin Peaks | Develop requirements and architecture together | Iterates, but keeps them as separate documents |
| "Fake it" (Parnas & Clements) | Iterate in practice, document as if top-down | Every change lands in the right document |
| Axiomatic design (Suh) | Alternate requirement and design at each level | Makes the loop explicit, one level at a time |
| Set-based design (Toyota) | Keep several designs open, narrow slowly | Delays commitment until there's evidence |
| Zave & Jackson's model | The spec covers only behaviour at the interface | A fixed, technology-free middle layer |
| Problem frames (Jackson) | Describe the problem in the world, not the machine | Same idea, later extended to admit architecture |
| Information hiding, ADTs, Design by Contract | Interfaces hide decisions likely to change | Technology choices stay behind the interface |
| Ports and adapters, Clean Architecture | The core talks through technology-free ports | UI and storage become swappable adapters |
| Model-Driven Architecture (OMG) | Platform-independent model first | Separates "what" from "on which platform" |
| Specification by Example | Examples describe behaviour, not clicks | Specs survive implementation changes |
| SEI methods (scenarios, ADD, ATAM) | Measurable quality scenarios drive design | Makes design drivers and constraints explicit |
| Architecture decision records | One short record per significant decision | Each decision is visible, with a status |
| Arcadia (systems engineering) | Need analysis, then logical, then physical design | The customer approves the need; engineers own the design |
| Spec Kit, Kiro (AI tools) | Separate the spec from the technical plan | Gates, clarification markers, re-sync after changes |

### Twin Peaks

- **What:** requirements and architecture as two peaks, worked on at the same time. Nuseibeh describes it as a finer-grained version of Boehm's spiral model (1988).
- **Loop:** accepts it. Early solution work surfaces requirements, which suits what Boehm (2000) called IKIWISI ("I'll know it when I see it").
- **Useful idea:** "core requirements", the goals likely to last longest, which should anchor a stable architecture.
- **Trade-offs:** a stance more than a method. It says to iterate and keep the content separate, not how to decide or who decides.

### "A rational design process: how and why to fake it" (Parnas & Clements 1986)

- **What:** nobody designs top-down, but you produce and maintain the documents that an ideal top-down process would have produced.
- **Loop:** iterate freely. When something you learn invalidates a document, fix it and every document after it. "The documentation is our medium of design and no design decisions are considered to be made until their incorporation into the documents."
- **Rules useful here:**
  - Every requirements statement "should be valid for all acceptable products; none should depend on implementation decisions."
  - Gaps "should be explicitly indicated".
  - Developers "produce a draft document and get it reviewed and, eventually, approved by the user representatives."
- **Trade-offs:** the documents need constant upkeep, and they deliberately hide the messy history, so rationale needs its own home.

### Axiomatic design (Suh)

- **What:** requirements (functional requirements, FRs) and design (design parameters, DPs) are broken down together. A requirement can only be broken down after choosing the design that meets it: "Having chosen the DP1, we can now decompose FR1."
- **Loop:** a disciplined zigzag: requirement, then design, then sub-requirements, then sub-designs.
- **Trade-offs:** from mechanical engineering, and formal (design matrices). It implies that deep requirement trees inevitably carry design decisions.

### Set-based concurrent engineering (Toyota)

- **What:** keep sets of design options open and narrow them gradually. Toyota "considers a broader range of possible designs and delays certain decisions longer than other automotive companies do, yet has what may be the fastest and most efficient vehicle development cycles in the industry."
- **Loop:** avoids picking one design early and then patching it, which fails if "one picks the wrong starting point".
- **Principles** (wording from secondary sources): map the design space; integrate by intersection; establish feasibility before commitment.
- **Trade-offs:** exploring several options costs more up front. Built for car development with many teams.

### Requirements, domain knowledge and specification (Zave & Jackson; Gunter et al.)

- **What:** three kinds of description.
  - **Requirements:** what we want to become true in the world.
  - **Domain knowledge:** what's true of the world regardless of the system, i.e. assumptions.
  - **Specification:** the system's behaviour at its interface with the world, using only what both sides can observe ("shared phenomena").
  - **The test:** specification + domain knowledge ⊢ requirements. (⊢ means "together guarantee".)
- **Loop:** the specification is a stable middle layer. "To say anything else about the machine is regarded as implementation bias." "It is not necessary or desirable to describe (however abstractly) the machine to be built."
- **Ownership:** Gunter et al. split the obligations. The buyer answers for the environment side: the domain knowledge holds, and specification plus domain knowledge give the requirements. The seller answers for the system side: the program meets the specification. "They build their deal around S, which serves as their basis of communication."
- **On restating:** "Some requirements are already implementable, so they can be copied directly from R to S." The others differ because they mention things the system can't observe or control, and domain knowledge bridges that gap.
- **Trade-offs:** formal roots (logic). And where the interface sits is itself a choice: Zave & Jackson say their framework characterizes the results of exploring that boundary, "not the explorations themselves", citing Swartout & Balzer.

### Problem frames (Jackson)

- **What:** analyse the problem in the world, not in the machine. "The intrinsic domain properties bridge the gap between the phenomena mentioned in the requirement and the phenomena directly accessible to the machine at its external interface to the world."
- **Loop:** keeps attention on the problem. Hall et al. (2002) found that "even modestly complex problems can force us into detailed consideration of the architecture of the solution", so they extended problem frames to allow "architectural structures, services and artifacts to be considered as part of the problem domain".
- **Trade-offs:** the notation and catalogue of frames take learning. The 2002 extension concedes that existing architecture sometimes belongs in the problem.

### Information hiding, abstract data types, Design by Contract

- **What:**
  - Parnas (1972): start from "a list of difficult design decisions or design decisions which are likely to change", and give each module an interface "chosen to reveal as little as possible about its inner workings".
  - Liskov & Zilles (1974): abstract data types, used only through their operations.
  - Meyer (1992): a contract states what the caller must provide and what the supplier guarantees (preconditions and postconditions). It "protects the client by specifying how much should be done" and the contractor "by specifying how little is acceptable".
- **Loop:** decisions likely to change sit behind an interface, so changing them leaves the interface alone.
- **Trade-offs:** module-level ideas. Scaling them to a whole product's interface, and choosing the right interface, are judgment calls.

### Ports and adapters (Cockburn), Clean Architecture (Martin)

- **What:** the application talks to the world through "ports", each "a purposeful conversation". Technology-specific "adapters" plug into them. "A graphical user interface or GUI is an example of an adapter." Martin: "A Web UI could be replaced with a console UI, for example, without changing the business rules."
- **Loop:** use cases "should generally be written at the application boundary... regardless of external technology", which makes them "more stable over time".
- **Trade-offs:** "What exactly a port is and isn't is largely a matter of taste." Qualities that live in an adapter, such as look and feel, fall outside a port-level description.

### Model-Driven Architecture (OMG)

- **What:** a computation-independent model (the domain and its requirements), a platform-independent model (PIM: the system without a platform), and platform-specific models (PSM).
- **Loop:** separates the platform choice from the system's logic. One PIM can target several technologies.
- **Trade-offs:** independence is relative. "What counts as a platform is relative to the purpose of the modeler"; "the concepts of PIM and PSM are, therefore, relative." Böckeler notes model-driven development "never took off for business applications, it sits at an awkward abstraction level and just creates too much overhead and constraints."

### Declarative scenarios, Specification by Example

- **What:** concrete examples, often written as Given/When/Then, describe behaviour rather than steps through a UI. Cucumber's test for each line: "Will this wording need to change if the implementation does?" If so, rewrite it. "What if, in the future, users log in with a voice interface or a thumbprint?"
- **Loop:** the examples stay valid through big implementation changes. Adzic reports teams relying on these "living documentation" suites to rebuild core systems; one team "had to rewrite the core of the virtual agent engine from scratch".
- **Trade-offs:** staying declarative takes discipline, and examples cover cases, not everything.

### SEI methods: quality attribute scenarios, ADD, ATAM

- **What:**
  - **Quality attribute scenario:** "a short description of how a system is required to respond to some stimulus", in six parts: source, stimulus, artifact, environment, response, response measure.
  - **Attribute-Driven Design (ADD):** design the architecture in iterations from "architectural drivers": design purpose, quality attributes, primary functionality, architectural concerns and constraints. "A constraint is a decision over which you have little or no control as an architect", such as "mandated technologies".
  - **ATAM** (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method): evaluates a candidate architecture against prioritized scenarios to find risks and trade-offs. (Summary from secondary sources.)
- **Loop:** quality needs are stated in a measurable, technology-free form, then drive the architecture and test it.
- **Trade-offs:** heavyweight for small projects; the workshops and evaluations assume teams of people.

### Architecture decision records (ADRs)

- **What:** one short file per "architecturally significant" decision: "those that affect the structure, non-functional characteristics, dependencies, interfaces, or construction techniques". Sections: title, context, decision, status, consequences.
- **Loop:** "Not all decisions will be made at once, nor will all of them be done when the project begins." Records are added as decisions are made, and a reversed decision is marked "superseded" rather than deleted.
- **Ownership:** the status records agreement: "proposed" until the stakeholders agree, then "accepted".
- **Trade-offs:** only works if writing them is routine, and it doesn't say who decides.

### Arcadia (systems engineering)

- **What:** a model-based method from Thales, now an AFNOR standard, with "a clear distinction between need and solution". Its levels: operational need analysis; system need analysis (what the system does at its boundary with users and other systems); logical architecture (a "notional solution"); and physical architecture, where "technical and technological constraints and choices" come in.
- **Loop:** one of its golden rules: "Check requirements against an architectural design model (early architecture) for robustness and feasibility." Need analysis can "renegotiate" customer requirements.
- **Ownership:** the two need-analysis levels "'specify' the subsequent design, and therefore should be approved/validated with the Customer."
- **Trade-offs:** built for large systems engineering with model tooling (Capella).

### AI spec-driven tools: Spec Kit and Kiro (docs read October 2026)

- **GitHub Spec Kit:**
  - The spec (what and why) is separate from the plan (how). The spec template says to "Avoid HOW to implement (no tech stack, APIs, code structure)", and that success criteria "must be technology-agnostic and measurable". The plan names the project type ("library/cli/web-service/mobile-app/…") and holds the technical "contracts/".
  - Anything unclear becomes "[NEEDS CLARIFICATION: specific question]" rather than a guess.
  - Feedback runs both ways: "When an architect discovers a better pattern, the PRD updates to reflect new possibilities." It also offers "Branching for Exploration: Generate multiple implementation approaches from the same specification".
- **Kiro:**
  - Three files with an approval gate after each: requirements.md (in EARS form: "WHEN … THE SYSTEM SHALL …"), design.md (architecture, interfaces, data models) and tasks.md.
  - Two workflows: Requirements-First and Design-First. Its docs suggest a Design-First spec "to validate technical feasibility", then a Requirements-First spec "for full feature development". After design changes, it can "validate and regenerate requirements to ensure they remain feasible".
- **Practitioner caution (Böckeler 2025):** separating the functional spec from the technical one is the common aim, but "I don't think we have a good track record as a profession to do this well."

## How this could map to my workflow

> [!warning] Interpretation, not findings
> Everything above is what the sources say. This section applies it to my workflow as options with trade-offs. It doesn't recommend one.

### Vocabulary match

| Zave & Jackson, Gunter et al. | My workflow |
|---|---|
| Requirements (wanted properties of the world) | Requirements tree |
| Domain knowledge (assumptions about the world) | No explicit home today |
| Specification (behaviour at the interface) | Contract |
| Program on a platform | Implementation, including architecture and tech stack |

### (a) An architecture-agnostic contract

**Support in the sources:**

- Zave & Jackson's specification: only shared phenomena, no "implementation bias".
- Parnas' information hiding: hide the decisions most likely to change, and the platform is one of them.
- Cockburn's ports: a GUI is an adapter, so mobile versus web sits outside the contract. My note's to-do example (add a task, list open tasks, mark a task done) has the shape of ports, or of an abstract data type's operations.
- Martin's "independent of UI", MDA's platform-independent model, Spec Kit's technology-agnostic success criteria, and the rewrites in Specification by Example.

**What the sources say about the risk of restating the requirements:**

- **Some overlap is fine.** Requirements already stated at the interface can be "copied directly from R to S" (Zave & Jackson). Parnas & Clements' requirements document is itself a black-box description of the system's outputs, with no separate contract for the whole system.
- **They differ when requirements are about the world.** If my requirements describe my needs in the world and the contract describes the interface, the two shouldn't collapse into one, provided the assumptions linking them are written down.
- **Limits:**
  - "Agnostic" is relative to some set of platforms (MDA).
  - A technology-free contract can still be forced to change by what turns out to be buildable (Swartout & Balzer).
  - Where to draw the interface is itself a choice (Zave & Jackson).
  - The line is hard to hold in practice (Böckeler).

**Options:**

1. **Write domain assumptions next to the requirements**, for example "I check my task list every morning". Requirements, assumptions and contract can then be checked against each other.
   - For: shows why the contract isn't a restatement, and makes the human's side checkable (Gunter et al.).
   - Against: one more thing to write and keep current.
2. **Say what the contract is agnostic to**, for example "the same on a phone, in a browser or in a terminal".
   - For: makes "agnostic" checkable, since independence is relative (MDA).
   - Against: can rule out an option nobody thought to list.
3. **Use Cucumber's question as the rule for contract lines:** would this line change if the architecture changed? If so, it doesn't belong in the contract.
   - For: cheap, and easy for agents to apply.
   - Against: judgment calls at the edges, such as look and feel.
4. **Write contract lines as declarative Given/When/Then scenarios.**
   - For: they double as acceptance tests and survive rewrites.
   - Against: longer than a list of operations.
5. **Write needs that shape the architecture as quality scenarios in the requirements** (stimulus, response, measure). For example: with no network, the human can still add a task within a second.
   - For: if mobile versus web matters because of a need, the need is stated and the agent still picks the architecture.
   - Against: takes care to keep solution words out of the scenario.

### (b) Keeping architecture decisions with their owner

**What the sources do:**

- Make the split explicit: the buyer owns "specification + domain knowledge give the requirements", the seller owns "the program meets the specification" (Gunter et al.).
- A decision only exists once it's written in its document (Parnas & Clements).
- Mark unknowns instead of guessing (Parnas & Clements' explicit gaps; Spec Kit's NEEDS CLARIFICATION markers).
- A technology choice someone else imposes enters only as a named constraint, separate from the requirements (ADD). My workflow already does this: steering is the only place I name a technology.
- Record significant decisions with a status, proposed then accepted (Nygard).
- The customer approves the need analysis; engineers own the logical and physical architecture (Arcadia).
- **Warning from axiomatic design:** below the top levels, breaking a requirement down takes a design choice. A deep requirements tree can quietly carry design decisions, the same leak I worried about in the contract.

**Options:**

1. **Adopt the Gunter et al. split as my ownership rule.** Human: requirements, assumptions and contract together give what I need. Agent: the implementation meets the contract.
   - For: precise, and matches my ownership table.
   - Against: the human side is only checkable with written assumptions, as in (a) option 1.
2. **Decision records with a status.** The agent proposes architecture decisions as records, and steering says which ones need my acceptance.
   - For: every architecture decision is visible, with an audit trail. It's also a possible home for the agent's reason when it departs from a FAVOR or DISFAVOR.
   - Against: overhead, and the risk of rubber-stamping.
3. **Mark, don't assume.** While helping draft the requirements or the contract, an agent flags any line that would assume an architecture instead of writing it.
   - For: cheap, and catches leaks where they start.
   - Against: depends on the agent noticing.
4. **Stop breaking down a requirement when the next level would need a design choice.** It stays "sufficient as stated", and the detail becomes the agent's.
   - For: keeps the tree free of design decisions, and fits my rule of breaking down only when needed.
   - Against: requirements may stay vaguer than I'd like.

### (c) Where the loop could live in the agentic software factory

**What the sources do:** iterate with separate documents (Twin Peaks); build and try versions to learn (Brooks); check requirements against an early architecture (Arcadia, Kiro's Design-First); keep several options open (set-based design, Spec Kit's branching); and update every affected document after a change (Parnas & Clements, Kiro's re-sync).

**Options.** None of these names a tech stack:

1. **Feasibility probe before the contract is agreed.** The agent tries throwaway sketches of candidate architectures against the draft requirements and contract, then reports what's infeasible and what it would suggest. I decide.
   - For: catches unbuildable contracts early, Swartout & Balzer's first case.
   - Against: costs agent time, and a sketch can anchor the choice.
2. **Change requests upward during implementation.** When the agent hits a limit that forces a change, or makes a choice that suggests an addition, it stops and proposes a change to the right artifact (requirement, assumption, contract or steering) instead of adapting quietly. This extends my existing "stop and ask the human" rule.
   - For: the loop runs through me, so ownership holds.
   - Against: more interruptions.
3. **Keep the documents current.** After any accepted change, the agent updates every affected document so the specification reads as if it had been derived top-down (Parnas & Clements).
   - For: the specification stays trustworthy. That matters more in my workflow because I never edit the implementation, which Böckeler calls "spec-as-source"; she warns it may combine the inflexibility of model-driven development with the non-determinism of LLMs.
   - Against: ongoing maintenance.
4. **Keep options open.** The agent carries two or three architecture candidates until evidence picks one.
   - For: avoids early lock-in (set-based design).
   - Against: more work per feature.

All four need somewhere in the project environment to record proposed changes and decisions with a status. That could become part of the contract between the factory and the environment, alongside "some ticketing system".

content.text:
I researched the requirements–architecture loop problem and the known ways to handle it, and mapped them to the user's workflow.

The file is at `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-sandbox/7d135cf4-8d4f-5641-9212-859d8c08d94e/scratchpad/requirements-architecture-intertwining.md` (Obsidian Markdown, about 320 lines). The repo and GitHub are untouched, and I didn't edit the user's workflow note. I read pages with curl instead of the web-fetch agent, because forks can't spawn agents.

**Main findings**
- **The problem:** Swartout & Balzer (CACM 1982, "inevitable intertwining of specification and implementation") first stated it for software. Nuseibeh's Twin Peaks (IEEE Computer 2001) is the standard name for the requirements-and-architecture version. Rittel & Webber's "wicked problems" (1973), Brooks (1987) and Parnas & Clements (1986) say the same thing, and design research calls it problem–solution co-evolution (Dorst & Cross 2001).
- **No known approach removes the loop.** They all manage it in one of three ways: iterate but keep the documents separate; put a technology-free interface in the middle; or make each design decision explicit and owned.
- **Support for the architecture-agnostic contract is strong:**
  - Zave & Jackson treat it as "implementation bias" if the specification says anything about the machine.
  - Parnas's information hiding, Cockburn's ports and adapters ("a GUI is an adapter", so mobile vs web sits outside the contract), and Clean Architecture all keep technology behind the interface.
  - So do MDA's platform-independent model, and Spec Kit's spec template ("success criteria must be technology-agnostic").
- **On the risk of restating requirements:** Zave & Jackson say some overlap is legitimate ("copied directly from R to S"). The contract differs where requirements describe the world, and domain assumptions bridge that gap. The user's spec has no place for those assumptions today.
- **Caveats from the sources:**
  - "Platform-independent" is relative, as both MDA guides say.
  - Implementation limits can still force contract changes (Swartout & Balzer).
  - Böckeler (Thoughtworks, 2025) says the profession is bad at holding the what/how line.
  - Axiomatic design shows that breaking requirements down deeply needs design choices. So the requirements tree can leak architecture decisions in the same way the user worried the contract would.
- **AI tools today:**
  - Spec Kit keeps the stack and its API "contracts/" in the plan, not the spec, and marks unknowns with [NEEDS CLARIFICATION].
  - Kiro offers Requirements-First and Design-First workflows. Its docs suggest a Design-First spec to check feasibility, then a Requirements-First spec for the full feature.

**Best fits for the workflow**
1. **Zave & Jackson's model, as extended by Gunter et al. (2000).** It backs the agnostic contract and explains why the contract isn't a restatement. It also gives an exact ownership split: the human answers for "contract + assumptions deliver the requirements", the agent for "implementation meets the contract".
2. **Twin Peaks plus Parnas & Clements' "fake it".** The loop happens, but each change lands in its own document, and "no design decisions are considered to be made until their incorporation into the documents". That keeps the spec trustworthy in a workflow where the human never edits the code.
3. **Decision records with a proposed/accepted status (Nygard), plus ADD's "constraints".** Architecture decisions stay visible and with their owner. A technology choice the human makes enters only as an explicit constraint, which is what the user's steering already does. The records could also hold the agent's reasons for departing from a FAVOR or DISFAVOR.

**Not verified:** ATAM details (SEI's report was blocked), the exact wording of Toyota's set-based principles (paywalled), and the full texts of Swartout & Balzer, Dorst & Cross, Hall et al. and Liskov & Zilles. For those I checked abstracts only. The file's sources list marks how each source was checked.
